questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with complaints of rhinorrhea, cough, and nasal congestion for 4 days. He was not experiencing severe headaches or problems with his vision. On physical exam, his vital signs were stable, and he was afebrile. He had some sinus tenderness to palpation but no periorbital edema present.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: Observation The patient has sinusitis. The most likely cause of this syndrome is a virus and would not warrant antibiotic therapy. The exception would be if the patient has an extended duration of symptoms (normally >7 days). The patient does not present with evidence of complications of sinusitis, such as severe headaches, visual disturbances, or neurologic deficits that would warrant ENT consultation or additional imaging. The best answer to the question would be just observation at this time.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q14

needs: Chapter 93 — Subdural Empyema, Epidural Abscess, and Suppurative Thrombophlebitis
questions.question: Patient upper resp infection/sinus. A few weeks later, headache, low grade fever.

parts.text: What is the name of the syndrome and complication (as seen on the image provided - picture of forehead abscess and a subdural abscess - Pott's puffy tumor)
What is the organism or group of organisms that is the most likely pathogen

questions.model_answer:
a) Syndrome/complication: Pott's puffy tumor (frontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal frontal abscess) complicated by an associated subdural empyema, arising from frontal sinusitis.
b) Most likely pathogen/group: Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group.
c) 4 other common organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, anaerobes (Fusobacterium and Prevotella spp.), and Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., Klebsiella, E. coli).
d) Empiric treatment: vancomycin + a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) + metronidazole.

parts.text: What is the anatomic structure that differentiates between preseptal and orbital cellulitis (0.5)
Name 5 clinical signs/symptoms that would suggest orbital cellulitis over preseptal (2.5)
Sinusitis of which sinus leads to highest risk for orbital cellulitis and why (1)
Patient now has ipsilateral lateral nerve palsy. What complication are you worried about (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Anatomic structure: Orbital septum - thin fibrous membrane serving as barrier between superficial lids and orbit; infections anterior to septum are preseptal, posterior are orbital (Mandell's); preseptal involves only lids not the orbit, orbital cellulitis involves soft tissues (fat, muscle) within bony orbit. Signs of orbital cellulitis: Proptosis; Painful extraocular eye movement; Ophthalmoplegia; Diplopia; Chemosis. Highest risk sinus: Ethmoid - separated from orbit by thin lamina papyracea (medial wall of orbit), contains multiple foramina for nerves/vessels, some people have natural defects; nearly all periosteal abscesses secondary to ethmoid sinusitis. Complication to rule out with cranial nerve palsy: Cavernous sinus thrombosis - spread to opposite eye through cavernous sinus usually within 24-48 hours of initial unilateral orbital findings; may present with bilateral findings or signs of bilateral neuropathies of CN III, IV, VI without lid edema/erythema typical of orbital cellulitis, especially from skin infections of middle third of face or dental infections
